With those dear burdens to their camp they pass,
Yet would not that dead seeming knight awake,
At last he deeply groaned, which token was
His feeble soul had not her flight yet take :
The other lay a still and heavy mass,
Her spirit had that earthen cage forsake ;
Thus were they brought, and thus they placéd were
In sundry rooms, yet both adjoining near.

<margin>74</margin>
All skill and art his careful servants used
To life again their dying lord to bring,
At last his eyes unclosed, with tears suffused,
He felt their hands and heard their whispering,
But how he thither came long time he mused,
His mind astonished was with everything ;
He gazed about, his squires in fine he knew,
Then weak and woeful thus his plaints out threw :

<margin>75</margin>
" What, live I yet ? and do I breathe and see
Of this accurséd day the hateful light ?
This spiteful ray which still upbraideth me
With that accurséd deed I did this night,
Ah, coward hand, afraid why should'st thou be,
Thou instrument of death, shame and despite,
Why should'st thou fear, with sharp and trenchant knife,
To cut the thread of this blood-guilty life ?

<margin>76</margin>
" Pierce through this bosom, and my cruel heart
In pieces cleave, break every string and vein ;
But thou to slaughters vile which uséd art,
Think'st it were pity so to ease my pain :
Of luckless love therefore in torments' smart
A sad example must I still remain,
A woeful monster of unhappy love,
Who still must live, lest death his comfort prove :

<margin>77</margin>
" Still must I live in anguish, grief, and care ;
Furies my guilty conscience that torment,
The ugly shades, dark night, and troubled air
In grisly forms her slaughter still present,
Madness and death about my bed repair,
Hell gapeth wide to swallow up this tent ;
Swift from myself I run, myself I fear,
Yet still my hell within myself I bear.

Es lebe die Geschichtszeichnung großen Styls!

Bisher sind wir von der Voraussetzung ausgegangen, Herrn Dühring’s hartnäckiges Falschcitiren sei wenigstens in gutem Glauben geschehen und beruhe entweder auf einer ihm eigenen totalen Unfähigkeit des Verständnisses, oder aber auf einer, der Geschichtszeichnung großen Stils eigenthümlichen und sonst wohl als liederlich bezeichneten Gewohnheit, aus dem Gedächt-

And so that the matter might be graspable even for children of six years, Marx assumes on page 56 an "association of free men, who work with common means of production and consciously expend their individual labor-powers as a single social labor-power," that is, a socialistically organized association, and says: "The total product of the association is a social product. It must therefore be distributed among them." And that is certainly clear enough, even for the "Hegelianized" head of Mr. Dühring.

The "simultaneously individual and social property," this confused hermaphroditic shape, this absurdity that must allegedly emerge from Hegelian dialectics, this fog-world, this profound dialectical riddle which Marx leaves his adepts to solve—it is once again a free creation and imagination of Mr. Dühring. Marx, as an alleged Hegelian, is obliged to provide a proper "higher unity" as the result of the negation of the negation, and since he does not do this to Mr. Dühring's taste, the latter must again fall into a "higher and nobler style" and, in the interest of "full truth," foist upon Marx things that are Mr. Dühring’s own manufacture. A man who is so totally incapable of quoting correctly, even by way of exception, may well fall into moral indignation toward the "Chinese erudition" of other people, who quote correctly without exception but who, by this very fact, "badly cover up the lack of an insight into the whole of the ideas of the writers cited in each case." Mr. Dühring is right. Long live the writing of history in the "grand style"!

Until now, we have proceeded from the assumption that Mr. Dühring’s stubborn misquoting happened at least in good faith and rested either on a total inability to understand, which is characteristic of him, or on a habit peculiar to the writing of history in the "grand style"—and otherwise usually termed sloppy—of quoting from memory.
